lede: Four words change the whole question: given that. They tell you something has already happened, so the group you are choosing from is smaller than it was. Everything about conditional probability is deciding which smaller group goes on the bottom of the fraction.
can: Read a conditional probability off a table, a Venn diagram or a tree
Use the formula on the sheet, with the condition on the denominator
Spot when one event sits inside another, so the numerator is the smaller one

md:
200 people were asked how they travel to work and which age group they are in. 96 travel by bus and 80 are under 25.
Ask 'what is the probability a person travels by bus' and the group is all 200. Add 'given that the person is under 25' and the group is the 80 in that column. Nothing else about the table has changed.

prompt: On the travel table above, how many of the 200 people are under 25 and travel by bus?
explain: 42, the cell where the bus row meets the under-25 column. Every conditional probability in this topic is built from one cell like that.

md:
'The probability of bus, given under 25' is written $P(\text{bus} \mid \text{under 25})$. The upright bar is read 'given'.
The condition, under 25, is what has already happened, and it is the group you are now choosing from. So the denominator is the under-25 total, 80, and the numerator is the 42 of them who take the bus.

prompt: On the ringed travel table above, which total is the denominator of $P(\text{bus} \mid \text{under 25})$?
explain: The condition names the under-25s, so those 80 are the group you are choosing from. Dividing by 200 would ignore the condition altogether.

text: 2. The formula on the sheet says the same thing

md:
Page 2 of the Unit 3 booklet prints $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$.
With counts, both the top and the bottom are over the same total, so that total cancels: $\dfrac{42/200}{80/200} = \dfrac{42}{80}$.
That is why a table question can be answered straight from the counts, and why a tree question, where only probabilities are given, uses the formula as printed.

title: Why dividing works
md: Conditioning is rescaling. The condition's probability is the new whole, so dividing by it turns the joint probability into a share of the smaller group. That is also why a conditional probability can be larger than the joint one it came from.

prompt: In $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$, which probability goes on the bottom?
explain: The condition is the new whole group, so it is the denominator. The numerator is the probability that both happen.

text: 3. The same table, the other way round

md:
$P(\text{under 25} \mid \text{bus})$ is a different question. The condition is now 'travels by bus', so the group is the 96 in that row, and the same 42 go on top.
Same cell on top, different total underneath, different answer. Reading the condition before anything else is what keeps these apart.

explain: $\dfrac{42}{96} = \dfrac{7}{16}$. The condition is the bus row this time, so 96 is the denominator.

text: 4. A worked example, start to finish

md:
96 students take chemistry, physics, both or neither. 54 take chemistry, 40 take physics, 22 take both.
**Step 1.** Fill the regions: chemistry only 32, both 22, physics only 18, neither 24. They total 96.
**Step 2.** Read the condition. 'Given that the student takes chemistry' means the group is the 54 in that circle.
**Step 3.** $P(\text{physics} \mid \text{chemistry}) = \dfrac{22}{54} = \dfrac{11}{27}$.

text: 5. From a tree, where only probabilities are given

md:
A delivery van runs on wet and dry mornings. $P(\text{wet}) = 0.4$; the van is late with probability $0.25$ on a wet morning and $0.1$ on a dry one.
There are no counts here, so the formula does the work. The denominator, $P(\text{late})$, is the sum of every branch that ends in 'late'.

title: Conditional Probability
why: Conditional probability from tables and from trees, in the notation this unit uses. The reversed-condition trap and the nested-event case are the steps this unit adds on top.

prompt: On the van tree above, the wet-and-late branch is $0.10$ and the dry-and-late branch is $0.06$. What is $P(\text{late})$?
explain: $0.10 + 0.06 = 0.16$. Two separate branches both end in 'late', so they add.

md:
$P(\text{wet} \mid \text{late}) = \dfrac{P(\text{wet and late})}{P(\text{late})} = \dfrac{0.10}{0.16}$, one branch over the sum of both late branches.
The numerator is one branch; the denominator is every branch that satisfies the condition. Finding one of the two and stopping is the commonest way this part is lost.

title: What the reports keep finding
md: Candidates often reach the right numerator, or the right denominator, but not both, and the two are never combined into the fraction. Write the formula out with the condition named before you put any number into it.

prompt: Using the van tree, $P(\text{wet and late}) = 0.10$ and $P(\text{late}) = 0.16$. What is $P(\text{wet} \mid \text{late})$? Give a fraction or a decimal.
explain: $\dfrac{0.10}{0.16} = \dfrac{5}{8}$, which is 0.625. Giving 0.10 on its own leaves the division undone.

text: 7. When one event sits inside the other

md:
Three pens are taken from a case of 11 without replacement. Ask for $P(\text{all three blue} \mid \text{at least two blue})$.
All three blue **is** at least two blue, so the two events happening together is just the smaller one: $P(A \cap B) = P(A)$. There is nothing to multiply on the numerator.

prompt: On the nested picture above, 'all three blue' lies entirely inside 'at least two blue'. What is $P(\text{all three blue and at least two blue})$?
options: $P(\text{all three blue}) \times P(\text{at least two blue})$
explain: Every outcome with three blue pens already has at least two, so the two events together are the inner event on its own. Multiplying would treat them as unrelated.

text: 8. Expected numbers from a conditional probability

md:
A conditional probability scales a group, and the group it scales is the one named in the condition.
If 800 members of a club are under 25, the expected number travelling by bus is $800 \times \dfrac{21}{40} = 420$.
Using $\dfrac{42}{200}$ instead would scale by the whole survey's share and give a much smaller figure.

prompt: In the travel survey, 38 of the 80 people under 25 travel by car. A club has 800 members, all under 25. How many of them would you expect to travel by car?
explain: $800 \times \dfrac{38}{80} = 380$. The 800 is the group the condition names, so that is what gets scaled, and with the 420 by bus it makes the 800.

md:
Read the condition first and write down the group it names.
Use $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$, with the condition underneath.
Read a conditional probability off a table, a Venn diagram or a tree.
Tell $P(A \mid B)$ from $P(B \mid A)$, which share a numerator and nothing else.
Use the inner event as the numerator when one event sits inside another.

This is the last part of a probability question, and the one that separates the strongest. It is worded 'given that', or 'a person is chosen from those who', for two or three marks. The first mark is the right denominator; the last is the divided answer. Stuck: write the formula with the condition named, then fill in the two pieces.
